Precious Metals Quarterly 4Q2006     Gold 

# Gold 

## Recent trends 

Prices remained below $600 for the second half of September and for much of October.  Right at the end of October, the weakening in the US dollar and fears over a US economic slowdown, prompted by slower than expected US growth in Q3, caused the gold price to rise again.  It remained in the $620s for the first three weeks of November before attempting a further rise, which saw it challenging $650/oz in the first days of December under the impetus of a further weakening in the dollar.  This later rise was, however, only supported by dollar weakness (the price did not rise in euro terms) and was not sustained with the price ending the year in the $630–$640/oz range. 

- The World Gold Council reported that identifiable demand for gold in Q3 was just 3% lower (jewellery 4% lower) than a year earlier in tonnage terms, a much smaller fall than in the first half of the year and equivalent to a 37% rise (jewellery 36% rise) in dollar terms. Demand was slow in the first part of the quarter, started to pick up as the price stabilised and then soared in September and October. 

- Industrial demand performed well in Q3, with offtake 5% higher than a year earlier, thanks to strong electronics demand. 

- Exchange Traded Funds continued to attract new business in November, rising by 60 tonnes; the gain in December was lower at 14 tonnes.  Other investor interest was subdued, and there were reports of profit taking. 

- De-hedging by mining companies in Q3 was, as expected, considerably smaller than in the first half of the year primarily as Barrick had completed the exceptional de-hedging programme it had carried out following its acquisition of Placer Dome in early 2006. 

- The President of the European Central Bank, Jean-Claude Trichet, confirmed in November that central bank sales during the second year (ending 26 September) of the Central Bank Gold Agreement (CBGA) had been just 395.75 tonnes, over one hundred tonnes lower than the 500 tonne annual limit.  This is the first time that signatories have sold significantly less than the annual limit.  Outside the CBGA there has been little movement in reported central bank reserves but there appears to have been some buying in quasi-official reserves.

##### What sources of new supply? There are three sources of gold supply: mine production, from w hich net de-hedging has to be deducted (or net hedging added); net central bank selling; and recycled scrap. We expect some increase in mine production over the next few years due to the rise in the price but the very long lags involved in mine development w ill limit this increase in the short term. Dehedging, w hich has reduced effective mine supply to the market since 2000 w ill inevitably itself fall over the next few years, since so much de-hedging has already occurred, but current sentiment in the mining industry w ill prevent any significant grow th in new hedging. Central Bank Gold Agreement selling now w ell under its annual limit. Outside the CBGA some cautious buying is possible so net central bank selling should fall. If demand rises significantly, the source of supply w hich must therefore rise to meet it is scrap. In the absence of economic distress, this needs a rise in price to increase. ##### although the fall in the hedge book limits the extent to which de-hedging will support the price in the future... ##### Longer-term support for a price rise.. Gold has been in a bull market since 2001 and the question is w hether the retreat from the high of $725 in May is the end of the b

ull market or a temporary correction. Elliot w ave theorists believe that markets progress w ithin a secular trend in five phases, the first, third and fifth being in the main direction of the trend (in this case upw ards) and the second and fourth being temporary corrections. Many analysts believe that the current phase is simply phase tw o and that the market w ill shortly enter the third phase w hich often tends to be the strongest. This is supported by the market's shape - a loose pennant being formed - since it fell from the high. Technically the key issue for the future w ill be w hether gold breaches the $725 high and moves on upw ards, in w hich case there is further upside potential, or w hether it fails to do so and forms a double top w hich w ill be a sign of w eakness. On balance both the technical and fundamental analysis suggest scope for further strength. ##### More recently the dollar has again become the driving factor $/oz $/€

Precious Metals Quarterly 4Q2006 Gold 5 ## Forecast update: the importance of China _Raging demand from China has had a significant effect on many commodities - but so far its impact on gold has been limited. At first sight this might seem strange; after all gold and gold jewellery has a long history in China. There are several reasons for this: relatively little demand is for industrial use; the after-effects of the prohibition on gold ownership between 1949 and 1982; and the regulations which hampered the gold jewellery industry

and gold’s investment use from 1982 until quite recently. Potential demand is strong but its development will not be automatic._ ### **Per capita demand is small** In China, as elsewhere, a relatively small amount of gold – annual usage is barely into double figures when measured in tonnes – is used in industry. Thus gold has not benefited from the surge in Chinese industrial activity in the way that many other metals have. The vast majority of demand is for jewellery, which accounted for 241 tonnes in 2005 according to data published by the World Gold Council and compiled by GFMS Ltd. Net retail investment accounted for a further 12 tonnes. This enabled China just to scrape ahead of Turkey to become the third largest market for gold consumer demand (jewellery plus net retail investment excluding Exchange Traded Funds) at 253 tonnes, but it remained well behind India (722 tonnes) and the USA (377 tonnes). In per capita terms jewellery demand in China is the smallest of per head major markets: 0.19 gm per head in gm/head 2005 compared, for example, to 7 0.54 gm in India, 1.18 in the USA 6 or 2.68 in Turkey. Demand was in 5 4 fact higher for a while in the late 3 1990s, peaking at over 300 tonnes 2 in 1997, when buying was spurred 1 by high inflation and the 0 devaluation of the renminbi and jewellery was bought as a quasiinvestment. It fell back towards the turn of the century stagnating at around 200 tonnes for a few years before starting to rise again recently. China has very low jewellery consumption per head gm/head

### **An industry hampered by restrictions in the 1980s and 1990s** Gold has a long history of mining, adornment and monetary use in China (although it should be noted that it was the only large country which did not adhere to the international gold standard during the latter’s heyday at the end of the 19th and early 20th centuries). However, between 1949 and 1982 private ownership was banned. The ban was lifted in 1983 but while individuals were allowed to own gold there were heavy controls over supply, fabrication and distribution. 6 Precious Metals Quarterly 4Q2006 Gold Up to 2002 all gold mined had to be sold to the People’s Bank of China (PBOC), at a price set by the PBOC, which then allocated gold to jewellery manufacturers. When additional supplies were needed the PBOC imported them and again controlled the allocation. The internal price could at times differ noticeably from the international price, encouraging smuggling. Only state-owned companies were allowed to manufacture or sell gold jewellery and retail prices were also controlled. Foreign jewellery companies, while allowed to produce and sell other forms of jewellery, were subject to heavy r

estrictions on any operation regarding gold jewellery; these restrictions continued to apply to those from Hong Kong even after the 1997 handover.  Gold coins and bars could only be bought from jewellers, at the gold retail price including taxes on the value-added component, and gold bars could not be traded. 

These heavy restrictions were not conducive to the development of a market-orientated industry.  Gold jewellery design remained old-fashioned and customer service was lacking. Neither did it help promote an industry which was able to compete either with other jewellery products, which were not subject to such stringent regulation, or with other consumer goods and services. 

Traditional gold jewellery in China, _chuk kam,_ is 24 carat – virtually pure gold – and of ornate design.  As in neighbouring countries it is typically sold to the consumer by weight with a low mark-up over the international gold price.  Purchasers have the option of selling it back to the jeweller.  These characteristics give it a strong investment element, particularly in a country where investment options for the individual have been limited. 

The decade from 1985 to 1995 saw the renminbi devalued from RMB2.94= $1 to RMB8.35 =$1.  The same ten-year period saw a couple of episodes of high inflation with the annual average change in the consumer price index exceeding 18% in 1988 and 1989, subsiding to 3% and then flaring up again to reach 24% in 1994.  The combination of the devaluation and high inflation made gold a reasonably attractive investment option, given the limited investment opportunities available to individuals in China; while investment products such as bars and coins (other than commemorative ones) were not on offer the 24-carat _chuk kam_ was a reasonable substitute.  This provided some support for jewellery demand, which rose, reaching a plateau of 300 tonnes or more between 1992 and 1997. 

From the mid-1990s inflation subsided and fears of further renminbi devaluation disappeared, removing these motives for jewellery purchase.  Jewellery demand fell and then stagnated at just over 200 tonnes until 2003.  Gold did not therefore participate in the consumer demand boom in China’s rapidly growing economic hotspots. Why was this? 

Traditional gold jewellery styles in China are very ornate and often fussy.  They often do not appeal to the more sophisticated urban buyers, particularly younger ones.  White jewellery is often popular - and the growing interest in platinum from around 1998 following strong and effective marketing by the Platinum Guild helped encourage this. 24 carat gold cannot, of course, be any colour other than yellow.  The fixed prices at which retailers offered gold often gave them a slender profit line compared to other jewellery products, thus limiting the incentive

for retailers to offer gold products, while the effective obligation to repurchase gold jewellery could at times also pl

ay havoc with their cash flow. 

Perhaps most damaging of all was the limited marketing and product development.  The last years of the 1990s saw World Gold Council budgets severely cut back (as a result of the impact of the low gold price on mining company profits) and thus a decline in its promotion and support to the industry.  At the same time marketing spending on competing products was rising substantially as companies increasingly realised the potential power of the Chinese consumer. While this applied to competing jewellery products — platinum and diamonds took a growing share of the market – the main competition came from the broader competitive set of discretionary products and services, such as electronic goods, mobile phones, computers, luxury products, holidays, beauty treatments etc. 

### **Gradual de-regulation** 

In the late 1990s, with the prospect of China’s adherence to the World Trade Organisation in view, a gradual three-stage de-regulation programme of the gold market was introduced.  The first stage was the liberalisation of the gold supply system.  After internal prices had gradually been brought into line with international prices, the Shanghai Gold Exchange was established in 2002.  This replaced the purchase and allocation system run by the People’s Bank; commercial banks were licensed to import gold bullion for trading on the exchange. 

Stage 2 was the freeing of the internal distribution market.  This included steps such as the removal of price controls, the abolition of the licensing system for jewellery market participants, enabling banks to sell bars and coins to customers and allowing these products to be traded.  These steps were implemented in the current decade.  Price controls were lifted in 2001 and the market was opened up to foreign companies from the end of that year – by March 2003 most of the barriers to the gold jewellery trade were removed.  Banks were allowed to apply for a license to offer bars and coins from the end of 2004 although the tax regime was not settled until November 2005.  Stage 3, still to come, will be the liberalisation of the import and export of gold bars. 

### **The battle to win over the consumer** 

While the liberalisation of the jewellery market in 2001-2003 removed the restraints on the industry it needed to develop more vibrancy and competitiveness to take advantage of its newfound freedom.  It also faced a stiff battle for its share of the consumer’s purse.  While gold had been hampered by state controls and regulation, competitors supplying other discretionary goods and services had poured promotional money into the country leaving the gold jewellery industry with much catching up to do.  It also had a product with limited appeal to the young urban professionals whose incomes were rising rapidly and a profit margin that did not endear it to retailers.  Despite the booming Chinese economy, gold jewellery demand remained flat. 

An interesting perspective on the lack of c

onsumer interest in gold jewellery in China at that time comes from market research carried out for the World Gold Council in 2002. Women in a number of gold’s major markets were asked what they would choose if they were given $500 to spend on themselves and presented with a list of choices including gold jewellery. On average, 8 Precious Metals Quarterly 4Q2006 Gold 33% of respondents opted for gold jewellery as their first choice with the proportion being as high as 68% in India but the proportion in China was just 11%. The solution was to reform the product. 18-carat gold had only a minimal share of the Chinese market but it was to offer a solution. A World Gold Council initiative was to re-brand 18-carat gold as K-gold, introduce Italian-inspired design and launch what was almost a complete new product onto the market. 18-carat gold can be white (or indeed rose), thus tapping into the preference of many consumers for white jewellery. Better design enables the product to appeal to the more sophisticated urban market. The product is sold at a fixed price, rather than varying with the international price, and retailers have a better margin. Finally the characteristics of K-gold mean that the purchaser is much less likely to sell it back than the traditional _chuk kam._ K-gold was launched in Shanghai in 2003 and Beijing in 2004, with subsequent launches in other cities. It has succeeded in spurring gold jewellery demand in China and by 2005/2006 it had gained 15% of the total jewellery market, starting from almost nothing. While the traditional market has also seen a little growth in the last two to three years the majority of the increase in gold jewellery offtake from 201 tonnes in 2003 to 241 tonnes in 2005 was #### K-gold has taken a growing share of gold jewellery demand tonnes

due to the rise of K-gold. Research indicates that it has attracted new buyers into shops and that there has been limited, if any, cannibalisation of the existing _chuk kam_ demand. This is progress and it seems likely that K-gold will spur further growth in the market. In the first three quarters of 2006, Chinese jewellery demand remained steady compared to a year earlier, unlike that in many other Asian markets, which fell due to price volatility. On a much smaller scale there has also been some progress in retail investment. In the first three quarters of 2006 this amounted to 8.3 tonnes, nearly double that in the corresponding period of 2003. ### **Heavy potential – but much work still to do to unleash it** While the progress in both retail investment and in jewellery has been pleasing its magnitude and impact is small compared to the impact that China has had on a number of other commodities. Gold has started to overcome some of

the barriers that existed but there is more work to do. When in 2005 the World Gold Council repeated the market research it has carried out in 2002 the percentage of women declaring that they would opt to buy gold jewellery if Precious Metals Quarterly 4Q2006 Gold 9 given $500 to spend on themselves had risen from 11% to 15% — but it still remained well below the percentages in other markets. The potential for both jewellery and net retail investment is large. If consumption per head of jewellery were to grow to as much as that of some other East Asian countries such as Indonesia and Vietnam (in the 0.30 to 0.35 gm/head range) it would add around 200 tonnes a year to gold demand; rising to that of India (0.54 gm/head) would add over 400 tonnes to annual demand while if it rose to the level of Taiwan (0.99 gm/head) another thousand tonnes a year would be added. Given the disparity in incomes, Taiwan is not an entirely sensible comparator for the moment, and India, while a poorer country than China, has a stronger cultural affinity. Nevertheless even allowing for these factors there is clearly significant scope for higher jewellery demand. Net retail investment would also seem to have much more potential given the limited investment options currently available to the individual. Perhaps the key factor to unleash this demand is sufficient promotion and on-going proper investment in new product development, staff training and other marketing. The results of the last few years show that this can generate results but the competition, at least as regards jewellery, is very stiff. Promotional spending on gold, as a percentage of market turnover, is considerably smaller than for many competing luxury products and the range of goods and services competing for the Chinese consumer’s growing wealth is large. Under current circumstances an explosion in Chinese demand for gold does not seem likely.
